gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the wind input on Nature's Generator units is a 'shared port' with solar. On the L6000 the solar side is two inputs of 12–60 Vdc / 1,200 W each, so the '2,400 W solar + 150 W wind' that ChatGPT added up is probably not available at the same time; connecting the turbine likely leaves one 1,200 W solar input. That 150 W is also only reached at a 27 mph wind.
standout_why: I compared against our own dealectric.com page, which ChatGPT cited at rank 1, and ChatGPT's answer built on the cited Nature's Generator pages. Our page lists '150 W port' / '350 W port' as if wind adds to the solar figure and gives one output figure per unit, with no surge and no cycle life. ChatGPT's answer repeats '2,400 W solar input and 150 W wind input' as if both run together. Our page already has the 27 mph / cube-law point, so that part is not new. I could not open the cited US product pages (naturesgenerator.com gave HTTP 429 or a certificate error), so I can't rule out that they also say 'shared port' somewhere. The maker's help-center spec sheets do say it. The DOE Small Wind Guidebook PDF was not opened.
decides: It confirms the L3600 stays the pick among power stations with a wind port. It is the only model the maker lists as compatible with the 150 W turbine, and the turbine help page does not list the L6000. But it changes the table. Wind does not add to solar on these units: the port is shared. So the 'Max solar input' and 'Wind input' columns should not be read as additive. The footnote should say wind replaces solar on a shared port. For the L6000, the inference is that it then has about 1,200 W of solar plus up to 150 W of wind, and only at 27 mph. For a shopper whose site has good sun, adding a turbine costs solar capacity. That supports the 'solar-only unless you have strong steady wind' advice. A second normalisation for the table: the L6000's 4,000 cycles are rated to 70% capacity, while the L3600 and MyGrid publish only a cycle count with no end point.
